  - No Server Actions until the upgrade (owner decision 4): `build-hardening.spec.ts` fails on any `'use server'` in apps/web or packages/ (tests and scripts excepted), and the new CI step after `next build` (`scripts/check-build-output.ts`) fails on the directive, on any action in `.next/server/server-reference-manifest.json` and on any `.map` under `.next/static`. A second CI step asks the running app: `/_next/image?...&w=1` must answer 404 (400 while the endpoint was on), a browser chunk 200 and its `.map` 404.
- **Side item, public source maps: fixed.** Sentry 8 turns on source maps for every production build (`hidden-source-map`: no comment in the JS, but the files stay in `.next/static`, which Next.js serves to anyone). The `disableServerWebpackPlugin` / `disableClientWebpackPlugin` options in `next.config.js` were Sentry 7 options that Sentry 8 ignores, so "no upload without a DSN" never held. Now `sourcemaps.disable` is set unless `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN`, `SENTRY_ORG` and `SENTRY_PROJECT` are all set, and `sourcemaps.deleteSourcemapsAfterUpload` is always on (Sentry's deletion step runs even when the upload fails). Sentry deletes only `*.js.map`: a local build with an upload configured (pointed at an unreachable local address, so it failed) left two `.css.map` files, so `pnpm build` now ends with `scripts/remove-public-source-maps.mjs`, which removes every `.map` under `.next/static` (Railway's build command runs this script). Checked on local production builds: main's config left **65** `.map` files in `.next/static` (the build check fails, listing them); this branch leaves none, without an upload and with one (both pass).
- **Node 22 LTS pinned.** Root `engines.node` `22.x` (was `>=20.0.0`), `.nvmrc` and `.node-version` `22`, CI `setup-node` from `.nvmrc` (was 20). Node 20 reached end of life on 30 Apr 2026. How Railway's Nixpacks picks the version, and what to check after the deploy: [5.6](#56-deployment-on-railway), [5.12](#512-how-to-verify-a-deploy). A newer Node installs locally with pnpm's "Unsupported engine" warning.
- **E2, quick fix: partly fixed by this first version** (the review below found crafted files of a few KB that still blocked the app for minutes or crashed it, and a worst case far above the "about 2 s" this block gave; fixed there). The real isolation is assessment PR 5, a worker thread with a memory cap and a timeout that really stops it. Owner decision 16: 10 MB and 50,000 rows kept; 50 MB unpacked and 10 sheets added.
  - The 10 s "parse timeout" is removed: the parse is synchronous, so its timer could only run after the parse had finished. Comments and docs say so.
  - `lib/workbook-guard.ts` (`checkWorkbookZip`) walks the .xlsx zip the way SheetJS does and unpacks each part with zlib under a hard cap, so the size is measured, never taken from the headers (SheetJS allocates by the header size and unpacks to the end of the stream whatever it says). Refused before SheetJS sees the file: over 50 MB unpacked, over 1,000 parts, a part whose header size is not its real size, a password-protected part, an archive that is not an Excel workbook (OpenDocument, Numbers, an archive inside; SheetJS would unpack those further).
  - The sheet count comes from a first SheetJS pass that reads only the workbook's sheet list (`bookSheets`); more than 10 sheets are refused before any sheet is read.
  - Each sheet is read to at most `READ_ROWS` = 50,100 rows (`sheetRows`; CSV: Papa `preview`). A sheet cut there is never shortened without a word: the sheet that is read is refused, another is named "N rows or more" in the warning.
  - SheetJS now gets a Buffer view of the upload: given a Uint8Array it copied the rest of the file for every part it unpacked (5,000 small parts: 8.4 s in the sheet-list pass alone; with a Buffer 65 ms).
  - Measured on the maintainer's machine with `parseUpload` (event loop blocked / memory): a 606 KB workbook unpacking to 200 MB, more than 3 min before, **31 ms** now (refused); the same with headers claiming 4 KB, 0.7 s reading 0 rows before, 28 ms refused now; a 138 KB workbook unpacking to 45 MB (1.15 M rows; not the worst the caps allow, see the review block below), 9.0 s and 877 MB before, **1.9 s and 382 MB** now; a 120,000-row sheet 0.65 s → 0.60 s; a 9.8 MB CSV of 1.29 M tiny rows 2.4 s → 0.56 s. Local order files (the real-data file of 26 Sep and the file of 25 Sep in `.dev/`, the `orders-150.xlsx` fixture, the S04 / S05 scenario files): 0.08-0.72 MB unpacked, 10-16 parts, 1 sheet, 11-154 ms, far under the caps.
  - Behaviour changes a dispatcher can see: the new refusal messages (above); a sheet with 50,000 rows or fewer that goes on past row 50,100 (empty rows, or an Excel used range that runs on) is refused with "If the rows below your data are empty, delete them"; empty lines in a CSV count towards the 50,100 lines read; RouteIQ's own plan workbook (20-22 sheets) cannot be uploaded back (no upload expects it).
- **Tests** (each checked to fail without its fix, by reverting that part): `upload-limits.spec.ts` (19): without the zip check 6 fail, without `sheetRows` 5, without the sheet count 1, with a Uint8Array 1, without `preview` 1, ignoring the cut 3, with a timer armed again 1. `build-hardening.spec.ts` (16): main's `next.config.js` fails 5, a `'use server'` in `lib/` fails the repo guard, main's `package.json`, `ci.yml` and no `.nvmrc` fail the Node and CI checks, a build script without the map removal fails 1. The CI script was run on real local builds: main's config fails (65 maps), a probe page with an inline Server Action fails twice (the directive and the manifest id), this branch passes, also through `pnpm build` with a failing Sentry upload (the removal step took the 2 CSS maps Sentry left). Counts: [5.3](#53-test-suites).
- **Owner actions.** Build on staging first if one exists, then check the Node version in the web build log ([5.6](#56-deployment-on-railway)); after the deploy, the two 404 checks of [5.12](#512-how-to-verify-a-deploy) step 12 (the source-map check is also the audit's read-only production check); check that NMWC's largest real order and customer files pass (only local copies were measured). The app binds to localhost on the Windows PC (decision 4, applied in A1 v2: the dev script is `next dev -H 127.0.0.1`; use `next start -H 127.0.0.1` for a local production run).
- **Still open.** The parse still runs on the event loop (assessment PR 5); what a file near the caps still costs is in the review block below (5-11 s; this block said "about 2 s", measured on one file). Everything else in F01 waits for the Next.js 16 upgrade (assessment PR 9). (P5 later fixed this: every upload is read in a separate process with a time limit and a heap cap; see its block, the last one.)

**A1 review fixes** (same branch, `audit-1-hardening`; review of the A1 diff: five findings, each confirmed by two reviewers with their own files, in `.dev/scratch-a1-v1/`). No migration, no new or changed API route (the role matrix is unchanged: the three upload routes answer 400 with the message, as before), no solver change. All in `lib/workbook-guard.ts` (`guardSpreadsheet`, `checkWorkbookZip`) and `lib/csv.ts` (`parseExcelSheets`, `sheetRanges`, `pickSheet`).

- *E2 was not closed: a 1.6-4 KB workbook still blocked the app for minutes or crashed it, because the sheet's range width was never capped* (high). `sheet_to_json` visits every cell of a sheet's range and, with `defval`, gives every row a key per column; the width comes from the size record or the right-most cell, and `sheetRows` cuts only rows. The reviewers' 1,632-byte file with `<dimension ref="A1:XFD2000"/>` and 2 rows took 28 s and 641 MB (A1:XFD50000: still running at 120 s); one header cell in column XFD with 200 rows 6.1 s, with 2,000 rows a V8 out-of-memory crash (which drops every request in flight and can leave a day on "optimizing", F09). A 43 KB workbook with a 16,384-column header row took 33 s; ten sheets of 50,000 rows 6 s. **Fixed:** before any sheet is turned into rows, each sheet's range (decoded as `sheet_to_json` decodes it) is checked (`sheetRanges`): a range wider than 200 columns, or ranges adding up to more than 2,500,000 cells over all sheets, is first cut to the last row and column that hold a cell (only empty trailing columns, the `__empty` keys, and blank rows go; within the caps a range is walked as before); what is still over is refused, naming the sheet ("Sheet "Orders" has 16,384 columns; at most 200 can be read. Delete the columns you do not need, or save only the sheet you need as a new workbook or as CSV, and upload that." / "This workbook is too large to read: its sheets span N cells (rows x columns); at most 2,500,000 can be read. ..."). The size record is still read, so a sheet that goes on past row 50,100 is still refused, never cut. Now: A1:XFD2000 and A1:XFD50000 read as their 2 rows in 20-27 ms; the XFD-cell files refused in 46 / 210 ms; the 16,384-column header refused in 0.15 s; 200 columns x 50,000 rows (8.8 s) refused in 0.3 s.
- *The "archive inside" refusal and the 50 MB cap could be bypassed: the check read part names from the zip's central directory, SheetJS reads them from each part's local header* (medium). A part named "[Content_Types].xml" in the directory and "Index.zip" in its header passed the check (1 part, 1.2 MB), and SheetJS opened it as a workbook of its own: the reviewers' 1.2 MB file unpacked to about 400 MB inside SheetJS (14.6 s, 1.7 GB; the inner workbook alone is refused in 31 ms). **Fixed:** `checkWorkbookZip` reads each part's name from its local header and refuses a part whose two names differ ("damaged"); the checks use that name as SheetJS finds parts: by path with "/" or "\" (a "META-INF\manifest.xml" made SheetJS read the file as OpenDocument) and by file name with a trailing "/" dropped ("Index.zip/"); a name with a control character is refused as damaged. The reviewers' file is refused in 3 ms.
- *A 1.7 KB workbook with one hyperlink over a large range blocked the app for minutes* (medium). SheetJS makes a cell object for every address of a link's range (`parse_ws_xml_hlinks`), whatever `sheetRows` says. A1:T200000: 5.6 s and 977 MB; A1:XFD1048576 (17 billion cells): still running at 180 s. The same holds in the other formats: an .xls link record is looped over cell by cell (a 4 KB .xls with one link over 65,536 x 65,536 cells: about half an hour; 2,000 x 2,000 took 2 s), and so is a link in a binary (.xlsb) sheet, which SheetJS reads from any worksheet part whose name ends in ".bin", also inside an .xlsx. **Fixed:** before SheetJS reads the file, the link ranges are added up and more than 200,000 cells in all are refused ("This workbook has links over N cells; at most 200,000 can be read. Remove the links (in Excel: select the cells, right-click, Remove Hyperlinks), save it and upload it again."): in every part of an .xlsx, read the way SheetJS reads them (its tag and attribute patterns, UTF-8 or a UTF-16 part, namespace prefixes, any case, "_" suffixes; a test compares the count with the cells SheetJS makes for each variant), and in the link and tooltip records of an .xls workbook stream. An address too long for a number (hundreds of letters) decodes to Infinity, and SheetJS's loop over it never ends: it counts as endless. Binary parts are hidden from SheetJS (a new central directory without them is appended to the bytes it reads; it needs none of them for an .xlsx: printer settings, macros, embedded objects), and a renamed .xlsb is refused ("This is an Excel binary workbook (.xlsb), which cannot be read. ..."). Both link files are refused in 4-5 ms, the .xls in 20 ms.
- *The E2 docs promised a worst case of about 2 s* (medium, docs). That figure came from one 45 MB single-sheet file; files that passed every cap blocked the app for 6-33 s or more. `docs/SECURITY.md` section 10, `DISPATCHER_GUIDE.md`, `admin.md`, this handbook ([2.2](#22-the-web-app), [2.8](#28-timeouts-budgets-and-limits), [3.3](#33-step-1-upload-and-validate-the-order-file), [7.2](#72-known-limitations), the A1 block above) and the `csv.ts` / `workbook-guard.ts` comments now give the measured cost of the largest files the caps allow (below) and say that only PR 5 bounds the time. `repo-guards.spec.ts` refuses the old wordings in `docs/` and `lib/`.
- *A blank but formatted first sheet was picked and refused where main read the data sheet* (low). A sheet cut at row 50,100 counted as holding data whatever its first rows were, so a first sheet with no value and a used range to row 60,000 (formatting) was chosen over the customer list on sheet 2 and refused with "Too many rows ... delete the empty rows"; an order upload named it as "(0 rows or more)". **Fixed:** a sheet whose first 50,100 rows hold no value is empty, cut or not: it is not read, not a candidate and not named (`parseExcelSheets` keeps only sheets with rows, `pickSheet` counts only rows with a value). The chosen sheet that goes on past row 50,100 is still refused.
- **Found while fixing (same cause: SheetJS does far more work than the file's size; not in the review):**
  - *SheetJS's other readers.* It picks its reader from the first bytes, whatever the file's name or type: a 763-byte flat OpenDocument file named orders.xls (one cell repeated 1,000 x 2,000 times) took 7.7 s, and larger ones run out of memory; its web-page reader compares every cell with every merged cell (0.7 MB: 1.9 s, growing with the square). **Fixed:** `guardSpreadsheet` mirrors SheetJS's choice of reader (`sheetjsReader`, the same tests in the same order as `readSync`) and lets it read only a zip that is an Excel workbook, an .xls (a compound file with a Workbook or Book stream, or a bare BIFF stream) and text it reads as CSV; text that starts with "<" (after spaces, line breaks or a byte-order mark, also UTF-16) is refused as "a web page or an XML file", SYLK, DIF, Lotus, dBASE, RTF and SocialCalc files as "not an Excel workbook". A CSV sent as Excel (Windows browsers do) is still read by SheetJS, as before (the A1 review's SYLK test wrongly refused a CSV whose first header is exactly "ID"; the A1 v2 review below fixed that, and the crafted-.xls hole too).
  - *Millions of cells.* SheetJS's CSV reader tries every value as a number and as a date: a 9.5 MB CSV sent as Excel with 5 million cells took 20 s; a dense 39 MB .xlsx (2.55 million cells) took 11 s before the range check could refuse it. **Fixed:** both are counted before SheetJS reads them (the CSV's separators and line breaks, the .xlsx's cell tags that do not close themselves, so formatted empty cells never count) and more than 2,500,000 are refused ("This file is too large to read: it has about N cells ...") in 60-350 ms.
  - *Array formulas.* With formulas on, SheetJS compares every array-formula cell with every array formula before it (20,000 rows, a 275 KB file: 2.6 s, growing with the square). **Fixed:** `cellFormula: false`; formulas are not used, their saved values are read as before (20,000 rows: 0.33 s). A formula cell without a saved value (some generators write none) now reads as blank; it read as 0.
  - *Comments.* SheetJS checks every comment already on a cell before adding one: 20,000 on one cell took 0.4 s, and 50 MB of them would take minutes. **Fixed:** more than 10,000 comments are refused before SheetJS reads the workbook.
- **Behaviour changes a dispatcher can see:** the new refusals above, each saying what to do (NMWC's real files are far from all of them); a formula without a saved value reads as blank instead of 0; a blank formatted sheet is ignored instead of refused; a sheet over the column or cell cap loses only its empty trailing "__empty" columns (seen only in "Found columns: ..."). The local real files (the real-data order file of 26 Sep, the file of 25 Sep, their CSV export as `text/csv` and as Excel, the customer CSV, the late-order CSV) give the same rows, sheet and warnings as main; RouteIQ's own 26-sheet plan workbook is refused for its sheets, as in A1.
- **What a file near the caps still costs** (the maintainer's machine; times vary by about a third from run to run): an .xlsx of 50,000 rows x 49 columns (0.19 MB, 37 MB unpacked, just under 2,500,000 cells) 9-10 s and about 1 GB of memory; the same rows as CSV sent as Excel 7-11 s and 1.2 GB; ten sheets of 50,000 rows x 3 columns 5-6 s; a 45 MB sheet of 1.15 M rows (refused for its rows) 1.8 s; NMWC's shape at the row limit (50,000 rows x 15 columns) 2.1-2.5 s. Every upload is still parsed on the event loop; only the worker of assessment PR 5 bounds the time. SheetJS has many readers: these checks cover the ways found so far in which a small file makes it do large work, not every way that may exist.
- **Tests** (`upload-limits.spec.ts`, + 27, now 46), each checked to fail with its fix reverted, by a script that reverts one mechanism at a time and runs only the tests that cover it: the range caps 4, the local name 1, the foreign names 1, the link count in .xlsx parts 3, in .xls 1, the binary parts 2, the formats 2, the CSV cell count 1, the .xlsx cell count 2, the comment count 1, `cellFormula` 1, the blank sheet 2. The whole-sheet link, the 65,536 x 65,536 .xls and the binary sheet with a whole-sheet link were not run reverted (they run for minutes or out of memory); their smaller siblings were. The endless range was run reverted as a script: still running after 20 s. The one test that passes reverted is meant to: a range within the caps is walked as before. Counts: [5.3](#53-test-suites).
- **Owner decisions.** New caps and rules beyond decision 16, applied as defaults because the high finding needed them: 200 columns per sheet, 2,500,000 cells, links over 200,000 cells, 10,000 comments, and an Excel upload must be an .xlsx, an .xls or CSV. 2,500,000 cells keeps 50,000-row files up to 50 columns; 1,000,000 would cut the worst case to about 4 s and 0.5 GB but refuse 50,000-row files over 20 columns. Questions in [7.5](#75-open-questions-for-the-owner).
- **Still open.** Every upload is parsed on the event loop: a file near the caps blocks every user for 5-11 s and needs about 1 GB (assessment PR 5). Checking NMWC's largest real files is still the owner action of the A1 block. (P5 later fixed this: every upload is read in a separate process with a time limit and a heap cap; see its block, the last one.)

**A1 v2 review fixes** (same branch, `audit-1-hardening`; a second review of the A1 diff against the verified assessment, four findings each confirmed by two reviewers with their own files in `.dev/scratch-a1-v2/`). No migration, no new or changed API route (the role matrix is unchanged; the three upload routes still answer 400 with the message). No solver change. In `lib/workbook-guard.ts` (`sheetjsReader`, `guardSpreadsheet`, new `checkCompoundFile` and `looksLikeSylk`) and `apps/web/package.json`.

- *E2 was still open for an old .xls: XLSX.CFB.read itself could be made to use memory and time that grow with the square of the file's size* (high). The `cfb` branch of `guardSpreadsheet` called `XLSX.CFB.read` before any check. SheetJS's `make_sector_list` starts at `dir_start` and, wrapping, walks and copies a FAT chain from every sector it has not yet seen as a chain start; a later walk can still walk *through* a sector an earlier one reached. In a file whose chains are stored in descending sector order (sector s points to s-1) every sector starts a walk down through all the sectors below it, so the total is about D^2/2 for D sectors, though each sector still has one predecessor and it reads as one ordinary chain. Measured on this branch in guard mode (`.dev/scratch-a1-v2/cfb/run.ts`): 0.5 MB 0.14 s / 358 MB, 1 MB 0.57 s / 1.1 GB, 2 MB 2.6 s / 4.1 GB; projected about 48 GB at 7 MB and about 100 GB at the 10 MB limit, so the container is killed and every request in flight is dropped. (On main the same 1 MB file crashes V8, so this is not a regression, but SECURITY.md section 10 (then numbered 9), this handbook and the code claimed an upload's work is bounded, which for .xls it was not.) **Fixed:** `checkCompoundFile` reads the header, the 109 header FAT addresses and the DIFAT chain (bounded, cycle-detected), then replays `make_sector_list`'s walk order counting sectors only (no copies) and refuses the file as damaged once the total passes a few times the sector count - a well-formed file's chains are disjoint, so its total is the sector count. It also refuses a directory of more than 16,384 entries (SheetJS's `build_full_paths` is quadratic in that). The crafted 2,000-sector file (about 1 MB) is refused in a few ms; without the check it takes about 0.6 s and 1.1 GB. A real .xls (ascending chains, as Excel and SheetJS write) is unchanged.
- *Regression: a CSV whose first column header is "ID", sent as Excel, was refused as "not an Excel workbook"* (medium; two skeptics wrote it up separately). `sheetjsReader` returned `other` (refused as SYLK) for any file beginning with the bytes "ID". SheetJS does not: it routes such a file to `read_wb_ID`, which tries its SYLK reader and, when that throws (with WTF off, as `lib/csv.ts` reads), falls back to its CSV reader. A CSV whose first header is "ID" (`ID,Customer Code,...`, or `ID;...` with data rows, or a tab file, or `IDNo,...`) throws in the SYLK reader on the first record and is read as CSV. Chrome and Edge on a Windows PC with Excel send every .csv as application/vnd.ms-excel, so a dispatcher's order, customer or baseline CSV with a leading "ID" column arrived on the Excel path and was wrongly refused (main reads it; the advice to "save it as CSV" brought back the same refusal). Reproduced in `.dev/scratch-a1-v2/idcsv/` and `regress/`; a 91 KB branch-errors CSV in Downloads starting "ID,S" was one real case. NMWC's current files (headers "SO Number..." and "code,...") were not affected. **Fixed:** `looksLikeSylk` treats a file starting with "ID" as SYLK (refused) only when its first ";"-separated field is exactly "ID" *and* the next non-empty record's type is a SYLK record type (ID, E, B, O, W, P, NN, C, F); otherwise it is delimited text, bounded by `checkDelimitedText`, and SheetJS reads it as CSV. A genuine SYLK file (`ID;PWXL` then `P;`/`C;` records) stays refused.
- *Owner decision 4 (bind to localhost on the Windows PC) was only documented; `next dev` still listened on 0.0.0.0* (low). The Next.js 14 CLI defaults `-H` to 0.0.0.0, and the dev script was `next dev`, so the Windows-only critical advisory could be reached from the LAN whenever the app ran locally. **Fixed:** the dev script is `next dev -H 127.0.0.1`; `start` (Railway) keeps no `-H`. `http://localhost:3000` still works, so `TEST_BASE_URL` and the integration run are unaffected. `build-hardening.spec.ts` pins that the dev script binds 127.0.0.1 and that `start` has no `-H`. `docs/SECURITY.md` section 10 and `docs/LOCAL_DEV.md` now state the rule as applied, including `next start -H 127.0.0.1` for a local production run.
- **Behaviour changes a dispatcher can see:** an "ID"-column CSV sent as Excel is read again (it was refused on this branch, never in production); the new crafted-.xls refusal (a real .xls is unaffected); no other change.
- **Tests**, each checked to fail with its fix reverted (by disabling one mechanism at a time and running only its tests): `upload-limits.spec.ts` + 5 (a descending-chain .xls refused as damaged in ms, a real .xls still read; an "ID"-column comma CSV read with key "id"; a tab file, an "IDNo" header and a semicolon "ID" CSV read; a real SYLK file still refused), `build-hardening.spec.ts` + 1 (the dev binding). Counts: [5.3](#53-test-suites).
- **Owner decisions.** Decision 4's localhost part is applied as its approved default. Refusing a crafted compound file and the "ID"-CSV rule are bug fixes to the A1 caps, not new limits (the .xls structural check has no dispatcher-visible cap; the largest real files still pass). The alternative of refusing every .xls (an owner decision NMWC has not made) was not taken.
- **Still open.** The event-loop cost is unchanged (assessment PR 5). Checking NMWC's largest real files remains the A1 owner action. (P5 later fixed this: every upload is read in a separate process with a time limit and a heap cap; see its block, the last one.)

**A1 v3 review fixes** (same branch, `audit-1-hardening`; a third review, of the A1 v2 fix `5ac4019` and, with fresh eyes, of the merged head `76ce2f5`: six findings, each confirmed by two reviewers with their own files). No migration, no new or changed API route (the role matrix is unchanged; the three upload routes still answer 400 with the message). No solver change. In `lib/workbook-guard.ts` (`sheetjsReader`, new `idFileReader`, `scanXmlPart`, `checkWorkbookZip`), `lib/csv.ts` (`parseExcelSheets`, new `MAX_METADATA`, `MAX_PEOPLE`) and the test fixtures.

- *A long number format on many cells ran the web process out of memory* (high). SheetJS made the display text of every number cell, parsing the cell's format again for each one (`safe_format`; `safe_format_xf` for .xls), though the app reads raw values (`sheet_to_json` with `raw: true`), and nothing capped a format's length. A 162 KB .xlsx within every cap (50,000 rows x 44 number cells in one 255-character format, Excel's maximum) ran for about 90 s and died with "JavaScript heap out of memory" at about 4 GB; 5,000 rows took 11-13 s and 2 GB; a 4 KB file with one very long format on 300 cells ran out of memory too. **Fixed:** `parseExcelSheets` reads with `cellText: false` (both passes), so SheetJS makes no display text. Values are unchanged (raw). Header names come from `format_cell`, which formats a header cell on its own: in General for an .xlsx, so a number in a header row with a custom format now reads as "2026" where it read "2,026.00" (an .xls header cell keeps its own format; NMWC's headers are text). Now 50,000 rows x 44 cells in the 255-character format take 10.9 s and 0.94 GB, the same as with no format (10.0 s, 0.90 GB); the test's 2,000 x 10 file 0.1 s instead of 0.9 s. The one place a cell's own format is still applied is an .xls header cell, at most 200 per sheet: ten sheets of 200 header cells in one 65,535-character format (the most an .xls format record holds) took 6.9 s in `sheet_to_json`, within what a file near the caps costs.
- *`xl/metadata.xml` made SheetJS do work that grows with the square of a small part* (high). For each future-metadata block SheetJS looks through every metadata type (`parse_xlmeta_xml`), and neither was counted. 100,000 of each (a 15 KB upload, 4.8 MB unpacked) took 28-30 s through `parseUpload`, 200,000 of each 138 s; about 1,000,000 of each fit under the 50 MB cap (about an hour). **Fixed:** `scanXmlPart` counts metadata types and future-metadata blocks, and more than 1,000 of either is refused before SheetJS reads the workbook ("This workbook has N metadata entries or more; at most 1,000 can be read. Save only the sheet you need as a new workbook or as CSV and upload that."). Excel writes one or two; the real fixture has one of each. A 10 KB file with 20,000 of each (about 4 s in SheetJS) is refused in milliseconds.
- *A threaded-comment person list multiplied the comments* (medium). For each threaded comment SheetJS looks up its author in the whole person list (`sheet_insert_comments`); comments were capped at 10,000, people not at all. 9,900 threaded comments by an author missing from 2.9 million people (a 142 KB upload) took 109 s; 1,000 against 1,000,000 took 3-11 s. **Fixed:** a person list of more than 1,000 is refused before SheetJS reads the workbook ("This workbook lists N comment authors or more; at most 1,000 can be read. ..."); with 10,000 comments the lookups stay under 10^7 (10,000 x 10,000 took 0.5 s).
- *Self-closing cells with a type got past the cell cap* (low). The count skipped every tag that closes itself, on the view that it holds no value. But SheetJS keeps a piece of a row as a cell when its tag has a type (`<c t="b"/>` is a FALSE cell) or a `<v>` follows the tag (`<c r="A1" s="1"/><v>1</v>`, `<c/><v>1</v>`), and it also cuts at `<c/` (`<c/t=b>`). A 133 KB .xlsx of 4.5 million `<c t="b"/>` (43 MB unpacked) took 13-22 s and 1.1 GB before the range check refused it; other variants took up to 36 s and 1.8 GB. **Fixed:** `scanXmlPart` finds, in one pass, where SheetJS cuts a sheet into pieces (each cell start and row end) and counts each piece with a type or a value mark as one cell; it may count a piece too many, never one too few. A formatted empty cell (`<c r="B2" s="1"/>`) is still not a cell, so formatting alone never refuses a workbook; an open tag with neither (`<c r="A9"></c>`, which SheetJS does not make) is no longer counted. A test compares the count with the cells SheetJS makes for twelve variants; a 26 MB sheet of 2.7 million `<c t="b"/>` is refused in about 0.6 s. The one-pass count takes about 0.3 s on a 45 MB sheet (the old one about 0.2 s). Pieces SheetJS drops still cost it time: 11 million `<c/>` (45 MB unpacked, a 160 KB file) took 6.1 s, within the 5-11 s a file near the caps costs.
- *A semicolon CSV with an "ID" header whose first ID is "C" or "F" was still refused* (low). `looksLikeSylk` took any second record that starts with a SYLK record type for SYLK. SheetJS reads a file as SYLK only when every record is valid SYLK, so `ID;Code;Qty` then `C;5;10` ("5" is not a C field), `F;maths;40`, or `E;5;10` then `1;x;2` are CSV to SheetJS, and were refused here. While confirming it, the reviewers found the reverse, which was a hole: the check read only the first 4,096 bytes and did not decode SheetJS's escapes, so "ID", 5,000 empty lines, then `C;Y5000000;X1;K1` (5 KB), or `ESC $3;Y3000000;...` (24 bytes; ESC "$3" decodes to "C") passed as CSV while SheetJS read them as SYLK and allocated millions of rows (0.3-0.8 s and 0.6-1.1 GB; 20,000,000 rows ran out of memory). SheetJS also does the work of every SYLK record before the one it gives up on, so `C;Y5000000;...` followed by a CSV line costs the same. **Fixed:** `idFileReader` replays SheetJS's SYLK reader over the whole file, record by record and field by field (the record types, and the field codes of C and F records, whose unknown values make it throw with WTF on), up to the first record or field it throws on. It counts the reader's costly steps: a row field grows the sheet to that row, a width field loops over its columns, a value after a format checks the whole format, and one step per record. The file is read as CSV when the reader gives up within 100,000 steps (a few ms and about 10 MB; a CSV takes a handful). It is refused as "not an Excel workbook" when it reads as SYLK, when the reader would do more, or when a record after the first holds an ESC character (no CSV has one). All the reviewers' files: the CSVs are read as SheetJS reads them, the others refused in milliseconds; a real SYLK file stays refused. Only the errors WTF raises are replayed: where SheetJS gives up earlier on another error (a value before any row, `ID;Qty` then `C;K5`), the file is refused here though SheetJS would read it as CSV.
- *Handbook 7.3 "Expected counts" still ended at A1's 1205* (low, docs). The merge added 1340 to [5.3](#53-test-suites) only; 7.3 was already behind the A1 v2 count (1211), and PR8, PR9, A2 and A3 never updated it. **Fixed:** 7.3 names 1211, the merge's 1340 and this block's 1350, and says that [5.3](#53-test-suites) holds the latest.
- **Behaviour changes a dispatcher can see:** two new refusals (metadata entries, comment authors) and more cells counted in crafted files; a semicolon "ID" CSV whose first ID is a SYLK letter is read; a number in a header row with a custom number format reads in General. The local files (the order files of 25, 26, 28 and 30 Sep as .xlsx and CSV, sent as CSV and as Excel; the customer, product, truck and late-order CSVs; `orders-150.xlsx`; the S04 / S05 scenario workbooks; a plan workbook) give the same rows, sheet, warnings or refusal as `76ce2f5`.
- **Tests** (`upload-limits.spec.ts`, + 10, now 61), each checked to fail with its fix reverted, by a script that disables one mechanism at a time and runs only its tests: the SYLK replay (the A1 v2 check put back) 3, `cellText` 1, the metadata cap 2, the person cap 2, the cell count (the A1 v2 count put back) 3 (the two new tests and one changed expectation in an existing test). Counts: [5.3](#53-test-suites).
- **Owner decisions.** The new caps (1,000 metadata entries of each kind, 1,000 comment authors) and the 100,000-step SYLK budget are applied as defaults, like the A1 review's caps: the high findings need them, and no real file comes near them. Question in [7.5](#75-open-questions-for-the-owner).
- **Still open.** Every upload is parsed on the event loop: a file near the caps still blocks every user for 5-11 s and needs about 1 GB (assessment PR 5). SheetJS has many readers and parts; these checks cover the ways found so far in which a small file makes it do large work, not every way that may exist. Checking NMWC's largest real files remains the A1 owner action. (P5 later fixed this: every upload is read in a separate process with a time limit and a heap cap; see its block, the last one.)

**A1 v4 review fixes** (same branch, `audit-1-hardening`; a fourth review, of the A1 v3 head `35c5b3a` with fresh eyes and against main: three findings, each confirmed by two reviewers with their own files). No migration, no new or changed API route (the role matrix is unchanged; the three upload routes still answer 400 with the message). No solver change. In `lib/workbook-guard.ts` (`checkWorkbookZip`, new `sheetReads` with its copies of SheetJS's lookups, new `sameSheetList`; `guardSpreadsheet` also returns the sheet list), `lib/csv.ts` (`parseExcelSheets`), the test fixtures and the docs.

- *Several sheets could name one worksheet part, so SheetJS read it once per sheet and every per-part cap was multiplied by up to 10* (high). The caps counted each part of the zip once. SheetJS finds each sheet's part through the workbook's relationships: the sheet's `r:id`, then the target tried as "xl/" + target, as it is, and next to the relationships folder, through a lookup that ignores capitals and takes "\" for "/". Nothing stopped ten sheets from naming one part. A 121 KB upload of 50,000 rows x 49 columns in one part, inside every cap, took 9-12 s and 0.7-0.9 GB when one sheet named it; named by ten sheets it blocked the app for 94-108 s and reached 3.4 GB before the range check refused it, and with a 2 GB heap the process ran out of memory. Any planner could send it to the three upload routes. **Fixed:** `sheetReads` replays how SheetJS's `parse_zip` finds each sheet's part (`[Content_Types].xml`, the workbook part, its relationships, `safe_parse_wbrels`, the three tries and the same lookup), and two sheets that read one worksheet part are refused as damaged before SheetJS reads the file. `parseExcelSheets` also checks that the sheet list SheetJS reads first is the one the guard replayed (`sameSheetList`), so the replay can never count other parts than the ones SheetJS reads without the file being refused.
- **Found while fixing** (the same cause: a part SheetJS reads more than once, counted once). For each sheet SheetJS also reads its relationships, every part they name as comments or threaded comments, once per spelling of the target (`comments1.xml` and `Comments1.xml` are two reads of one part, and each adds the comments to the cells again), and the drawing of notes (VML) that its `<legacyDrawing>` names; it reads an external link each time `[Content_Types].xml` lists it. Measured before the fix: a 3 KB file whose sheet named one comments part of 5,000 comments 20 times took 8.8 s (SheetJS checks every comment already on a cell before adding one, so 256 spellings of 10,000 comments would take hours); a 51 MB drawing of 400,000 notes shared by ten sheets (a 1.1 MB upload) 58 s, against 4.3 s for one sheet; a 45 MB comments part shared by ten sheets 4.7 s and 1.4 GB, against 0.7 s; a 20 MB external link listed 200 times 1.9 s, growing with the listings. **Fixed:** the replay counts every read, and a part read again counts again against every cap: its size (more than 50 MB read in all is refused with "its sheets read the same parts again"), its cells, links, comments, metadata entries and comment authors. The check stops at the first cap passed, so the replay itself stays within the caps. Where SheetJS would stop with an error the replay goes on, so it may count reads that never happen (the file is then refused, where SheetJS would fail on it anyway), never fewer. A differential check on 15,000 random crafted workbooks (sheet ids shared, missing, or named `__proto__`; targets in every spelling; comments and drawings shared; links listed again; the workbook in another folder) compared, part by part, what SheetJS read with what the replay counted for the 12,500 the guard did not refuse, and found no part that SheetJS read more often; with the comment or the drawing count switched off, it found under-counts at once.
- *Chart sheets made cells that the guard never counted and that ignore the row limit* (medium). For a chart sheet SheetJS reads the chart of its drawing and makes one cell for every point cached in it, with no `sheetRows` limit. A 3.1 MB upload whose chart caches 1,300,000 points (the guard counted 1 cell) read as a sheet of 1.3 million rows in 5-5.5 s and 1 GB; one point at index 4,294,967,294, in a 1.7-2.8 KB upload, made SheetJS walk an array of 4.3 billion slots for about 3 minutes. **Fixed:** a workbook with a chart sheet, a dialog sheet or a macro sheet is refused before SheetJS reads it: "This workbook has a chart sheet (or a dialog or macro sheet), which cannot be read. Delete that sheet, or save only the sheet you need as a new workbook or as CSV, and upload that." A chart placed on a worksheet is not a chart sheet and reads as before.
- *After the merge, the audit status line at the top of this handbook still said only A1 was fixed* (low, docs). A2 and A3 are merged in main too. **Fixed:** the line names A2 and A3 with their findings, and `repo-guards.spec.ts` checks that it names every audit PR that has a block in 7.4.
- **Behaviour changes a dispatcher can see:** a workbook with a chart sheet (a tab that holds only a chart) is refused with a message that says what to do; crafted files get the refusals above. The local files (the order files of 25, 26, 28 and 30 Sep as .xlsx and CSV, sent as CSV and as Excel; the customer, product, truck and late-order CSVs; the plan and scenario workbooks: 370 files, each read with and without the order-sheet test) give the same rows, sheet, warnings or refusal as `35c5b3a`.
- **Tests** (`upload-limits.spec.ts` + 12, now 73; `repo-guards.spec.ts` + 1): seven ways two sheets name one part (SheetJS itself shown to read the part for both), ten sheets naming one 49-column part refused in milliseconds, sheets with their own parts in any spelling still read, the sheet list read as SheetJS reads it (namespaces, quotes, escapes, UTF-8) and a different list refused; a comments part named 3, 5, 6 and 20 times (the 3 KB file refused in milliseconds) and one shared by two sheets; a 6.5 MB drawing of notes shared by ten sheets; an external link listed 60 times; chart, dialog and macro sheets refused, a chart on a worksheet read; the status line. Ten of the twelve and the status-line test failed before the fix; two check that normal files still read. Each mechanism was switched off in turn and the A1 v4 tests run: the refusal of two sheets on one part makes 2 fail, counting a part again 5, the chart-sheet refusal 2, the sheet-list check 1, the comment reads 3, the drawing reads 1, the external-link reads 1. Counts: [5.3](#53-test-suites).
- **Owner decisions.** Refusing chart, dialog and macro sheets is applied as a default, like the A1 review's caps: NMWC's files have none, and the upload screens read only worksheets. Question in [7.5](#75-open-questions-for-the-owner). The rest are bug fixes to the A1 caps (a part read again counts again; no new cap).
- **Still open.** Every upload is parsed on the event loop: a file near the caps still blocks every user for 5-11 s and needs about 1 GB (assessment PR 5); with these fixes that is again the most the caps allow. SheetJS has many readers and parts; these checks cover the ways found so far in which a small file makes it do large work, not every way that may exist. Checking NMWC's largest real files remains the A1 owner action. (P5 later fixed this: every upload is read in a separate process with a time limit and a heap cap; see its block, the last one.)

**A1 v5 review fix** (same branch, `audit-1-hardening`; a fifth review, of the A1 v4 head `53c58b8`: one finding, confirmed by two reviewers with their own files). No migration, no new or changed API route (the role matrix is unchanged; the three upload routes still answer 400 with the message). No solver change. In `lib/workbook-guard.ts` (`sheetReads`) and the tests.

- *The replay numbered the sheets SheetJS finds by number differently from SheetJS, so it counted another sheet's parts and never the last sheet's* (high). When the workbook's relationships do not name a sheet (so `safe_parse_wbrels` gives up), SheetJS reads the sheets from `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml`, `sheet2.xml`, ... or, when `xl/worksheets/sheet.xml` holds text (its "Numbers iOS" numbering), from `sheet.xml`, `sheet1.xml`, ... It tests the part's text as it reads it (`getzipdata`, which decodes a UTF-16 byte-order mark); `sheetReads` tested the part's size. A part of only a byte-order mark (the 2 bytes FF FE; also 00 FE FF, or FF FE and one byte) has a size but no text, so the replay counted `sheet.xml`, `sheet1.xml` ... `sheet(N-1).xml` while SheetJS read `sheet1.xml` ... `sheetN.xml`: the last sheet's relationships, comments, threaded comments and drawing of notes were never counted again. A 3.5 KB upload whose one sheet names a comments part of 5,000 comments under 20 spellings passed the guard (the same file without the 2-byte part is refused, "15,000 comments or more") and blocked the app for 10-22 s while SheetJS put 100,000 comments on one cell. The `xl/workbook.xml` fallback (a `[Content_Types].xml` that names no workbook part) had the same size test; there it could only count reads SheetJS never makes. **Fixed:** both are taken from the part's text as SheetJS reads it (`sheetjsText`, which already copies SheetJS's byte-order-mark handling). The reviewers' files are refused for their comments in milliseconds; a `sheet.xml` with text still gives SheetJS's "Numbers iOS" numbering. The suggested extra check (refuse when a numbered part the replay reads is missing) was not added: it would not have caught this case, where every part the replay read existed. A test instead compares, for seven kinds of `sheet.xml` part and one and two sheets, the part SheetJS reads with the one whose comments the guard counts.
- **Behaviour changes a dispatcher can see:** none for a real file. The fix changes only a workbook with an `xl/worksheets/sheet.xml` part or a `[Content_Types].xml` that names no workbook part; none of the 62 local workbooks (61 in `.dev`, the repo's fixture) has either. Crafted files of this shape are refused.
- **Tests** (`upload-limits.spec.ts` + 3, now 76), all three failing before the fix; each half of the fix, put back on its own, makes its own tests fail (the numbering 2, the workbook fallback 1). Counts: [5.3](#53-test-suites).
- **Owner decisions.** None: a bug fix to the A1 caps, no new cap.
- **Still open.** As after A1 v4: every upload is parsed on the event loop (assessment PR 5), and these checks cover the ways found so far in which a small file makes SheetJS do large work, not every way that may exist. (P5 later fixed this: every upload is read in a separate process with a time limit and a heap cap; see its block, the last one.)

**Audit PR A5 "Owner rules: correct locations, every order has a depot"** (branch `audit-5-owner-rules`, on main `22fe298`, which has A2 #42 and A3 #43). The owner's answers of 27 Sep 2026 (evening) to the questions A2 and A3 left open, recorded word for word in [7.5](#75-open-questions-for-the-owner). Both are standing rules the system **enforces**, not reports.

- **Depot rule** (owner, on A3's question whether to add a read-only check for orders or order files without a depot: "no, all orders must have depots linked to them"). One migration, `20260930120000_orders_always_have_depot` ([5.5](#55-database-migrations), with the owner's read-only pre-check): every order and order file without a depot gets one, best evidence first (its file; the one depot of the plans that held it; for a file, the one depot of its orders; the company's only active depot, else its only depot; the rest a per-company history-only depot `NO-DEPOT` "No depot (kept for history)"), one `DEPOT_BACKFILL` audit row per company that changed, then `Order.depotId` and `UploadBatch.depotId` are NOT NULL. It takes its locks first and retries instead of failing, so it cannot fail on real data or on a busy app (a failed migration blocks every later deploy, `P3009`); the migration test proves the lock with a write still running when the migration starts (A5 review). Nothing changes for NMWC: one depot, and every order already has it. What the app now enforces:
  - **An order file is for one depot, never a guessed one** (`intakeDepot` in `intake-server.ts`, [3.3](#33-step-1-upload-and-validate-the-order-file)): the depot chosen on Daily dispatch must be active (422 `DEPOT_NOT_ACTIVE`); without a choice (the legacy Upload orders page) the company's only active depot is used; none, or two or more, 422 `DEPOT_REQUIRED` with what to do. Before, the first active depot by code was taken silently, so a company with two depots could file orders under the wrong one.
  - **The history-only depot gets nothing new** (`Depot.historyOnly`): a file on it is refused at confirm (`batchDepotProblem`, never "reactivate the depot"); `PATCH /api/depots/:id` refuses to make it active and the truck and region routes refuse to use it (422 `DEPOT_HISTORY_ONLY`, `lib/master-data-delete.ts` words); the Depots screen shows it as **History only**, its Edit form has a note instead of the Active switch and it has no Delete button (it always has orders, so Delete could only deactivate it again); the onboarding truck picker lists active depots only (it listed every depot). The other pickers already listed active depots only (dispatch screen, Trucks, Regions), and planning, the late order, Bring forward and `POST /api/runs` already require an active depot.
  - **Every creation path passes a depot**, checked: intake confirm (the file's depot, `confirmIntake`), the late order (`depotId` required by its schema, an active depot, `late-order/route.ts`), a Bring forward copy (`carryCopyData`, the active depot on screen), the upload (`intakeDepot`); the synthetic seed (`prisma/seed-synth.ts`) did not and now does. The Prisma types make a new path without a depot a compile error.
  - **Dead null-depot handling removed, no behaviour change for orders with a depot**: the "orders without a depot when the company has one active depot" branch of `ordersInScopeWhere` (and its depot count per call), of the Bring forward window (`windowOrders`) and of the dashboard's `PLAN_ORDERS_IN_SCOPE`; the file delete's "orders without a depot block on any depot's OPTIMIZING plan"; `findSameConfirmedFile`, `batchDepotProblem`, `revalidateIntake` and `confirmIntake` take a depot, never null.
  - **What looks different after the deploy**: files that had no depot now show in the day screen's file list of the depot they were given (`day-overview.ts`) and count in its duplicate-file check (`findSameConfirmedFile`); a company with two or more active depots can no longer use the legacy Upload orders page (the answer says to use Daily dispatch); an inactive or unknown depot for an upload is 422 instead of 400.
  - **Deviations from the design** (each with its reason): step (d) uses the company's only **active** depot before its only depot, like `ordersInScopeWhere` did, so orders without a depot stay on the plan that already held them when a company has one active depot and inactive ones; the history-only depot is a column (`historyOnly`), not a code pattern, because a company may already have a real depot coded NO-DEPOT and PATCH could otherwise reactivate it at made-up coordinates; the legacy upload keeps the one-active-depot default (NMWC's Upload orders page keeps working) and refuses only when there is no depot to choose or more than one; the migration also writes audit rows, because Prisma does not print NOTICEs and there is no console access to production.
  - **Tests** (each fails without its change, checked by reverting it): web unit `orders-have-depot.spec.ts` (14), `intake-merged-rows.spec.ts` +1 (and the history-only depot in the confirm re-check), `dashboard-live-plans.spec.ts` (the scope SQL is exactly the plan's depot); fixture orders in `carry-over.spec.ts` got their depot (the planner reads only the depot's orders now); integration (library level, real PostgreSQL) `orders-have-depot-db.spec.ts` (6), `dashboard-db.spec.ts` without its depot-less order, and the fixture depots in `cross-tenant.spec.ts`, `legacy-data.spec.ts` (both run against a local web server) and `runs.spec.ts` (typechecked; it needs the solver); the migration test `tests/migrations/orders-always-have-depot.spec.ts` (7, on a throwaway database, [5.3](#53-test-suites)).
  - **Not in this part:** `GET /api/orders?depotId=` still filters by the customer's region depot, not `Order.depotId`; `POST /api/runs` counts `totalOrders` without a depot filter (legacy, display only); a screen to move orders from the history-only depot to a real one (they are history: nothing plans them).
- **Location rule** (owner, on A2's question whether a LOW-confidence reading must be moved by hand before it is saved: "its a standing rule locations should always be correct as part of sop no item will be delivered without location"). Recorded in [7.5](#75-open-questions-for-the-owner). No migration and no schema change. What the app now enforces ([3.4](#34-step-2-customer-locations-and-details)):
  - **Typing or pasting a location** (L1). In ADD LOCATION a reading that is not exact (`needsPin`: every LOW reading and the MEDIUM ones - map centre, fewer than 4 decimals (since the owner decision of 28 Sep 2026 of the zeros at the end one counts, as in the import: "A5 owner decisions" below), degrees and minutes only, swapped, outside the area) or that could not be read keeps **Save location** off, with "This reading is not exact. Drop the pin on the customer's exact location, then save.", until the dispatcher clicks the map or drags the pin. Before, Save was the confirmation and stored the reading as read, verified HIGH. The customer's saved pin (the dialog opens on it) is saved again as it is only when it is exact. The customer page's **Set location** opens the same dialog; its map with typed lat / lng boxes saved through `PATCH` as verified HIGH with no check at all (not 0,0, not the area). A2's guarantees are unchanged (late answers dropped, one request at a time, Save off until the text on screen is read).
  - **The server checks every save itself** (L2, `PUT /api/customers/:id/location`). A reading is read again with the same parser and no network call (`checkManualLocation`; a short link from the `resolvedUrl` the Read returned) and refused with 422 `PIN_REQUIRED` (with the plain remedy) or 422 `LOCATION_MISMATCH`; the source and confidence stored are the parser's, a hand pin is `MAP_PIN` HIGH. `PATCH /api/customers/:id` refuses coordinates (400 `USE_SET_LOCATION`), `POST /api/customers` refuses a pair that needs a pin (422 `PIN_REQUIRED`). The audit row `CUSTOMER_LOCATION_SET` keeps working and records the confidence and the check.
  - **Bulk paths** (L3). The customer import stores no pair that needs a pin: a new customer gets no coordinates (LOCATION REQUIRED), an existing one keeps its own when the file points at the same place (else, since the A5 review, its unconfirmed saved point is marked LOW and blocks until the pin is placed), and the row is listed with the reason (`locationsNotSaved`), not as an error. A verified location is still never overwritten (F05). Order-file stubs (`intake-server.ts`, `geocodeConfidence 'MISSING'`) and late orders (`late-order/route.ts`) store no coordinates at all: nothing to change there.
  - **Planning** (L4). A location that is LOW and never confirmed is treated like an invalid one (`isUnverifiedLowLocation`, `locationBlocksDelivery` in `customer-attrs.ts`): blocking `INVALID_LOCATION` on the day screen (the card shows "Saved location is not exact (low confidence). Drop the pin on the customer's exact location."), OPTIMIZE / RE-PLAN ask first (409 `LOCATION_REQUIRED`), "anyway" leaves its orders unserved with that reason. Confirmed locations and HIGH / MEDIUM imports not confirmed yet are planned as before (`LOCATION_UNVERIFIED` stays a note, by owner decision of 28 Sep 2026, [7.5](#75-open-questions-for-the-owner)). Before this PR nothing stored LOW; since the A5 review the customer import marks an unconfirmed saved point LOW when the file points elsewhere, also for a customer already on a plan (handled at LOCK / LOADING / DISPATCH since the second review, next bullet).
  - **Every path that puts an order on a truck or tells a driver where to go** (L5), checked one by one. The check that holds everywhere is `buildDispatchRequest` (`plan-service.ts`, `locBad = locationBlocksDelivery(c, area)`): an order of a customer without a usable location is never a stop, it is left unserved (`MISSING_COORDINATES` / `INVALID_LOCATION`), and `startDispatchOptimize`'s `gate` answers 409 `LOCATION_REQUIRED` unless the dispatcher says "optimize anyway". Stops (`RouteAssignment`) are created in two places only, `applyScenario` (from the stored option the optimizer returned for that request, with the planned pin in `stopSnapshotJson`) and `createNextVersion` (a verbatim copy of the parent's loads and stops, snapshots included); `route-adjust.ts` only updates, and refuses dispatch plans. So OPTIMIZE, RE-PLAN with locked / loading / dispatched loads kept (the frozen loads keep the pin they were planned with; the open orders go through `buildDispatchRequest` again), same-day plans (`plan-from.ts` changes only times), Bring forward copies and late orders (new `Order` rows, planned only by OPTIMIZE / RE-PLAN), split orders (split after the per-customer location check) and the driver PDF, Excel and WhatsApp text (the planned pin from the snapshot) hold without a new check. A customer's coordinates can never be cleared (a blank is "keep" in every route and in the import), so a planned stop never loses its pin, **but its customer can lose a usable location after planning** (A5 second review): the A5 review made the customer import mark an unconfirmed saved point LOW when the file points elsewhere (and a changed delivery area can put a point outside it), and neither the snapshots (they compare only the pin and the hours) nor the load status changes looked at it, so such a stop could be locked, loaded and dispatched, also after "Use instead" or from a failed re-plan's copy, while the import said "Nothing is delivered to them". Now the load status changes LOCK / LOADING / DISPATCH (`changeStatusTx`) check the customers of the load as they are now with the same predicate (`locationGate`, 409 `LOCATION_REQUIRED`, [3.8](#38-step-6-load-states)), and the day counts such customers on PLANNED loads as out of date (`outdated.locationBlocked`, RE-PLAN offered). Verified points and HIGH or MEDIUM points inside the area pass as before, so the 28 Sep demo's locked loads are not affected. The other path with no check was the legacy whole-run dispatch (`runs/[id]/dispatch`, May-2026 runs of the previous planner): it now answers 409 `LOCATION_REQUIRED`, dispatching nothing, while a customer on the run has no correct location.
  - **What looks different after the deploy:** ADD LOCATION asks for a hand pin for a reading that is not exact (and for a saved MEDIUM or LOW point, or a saved point outside the delivery area that nobody confirmed); the customer page has **Set location** instead of an editable map; an import lists "location(s) not exact" instead of storing them; `PUT { input }` answers `PIN_REQUIRED` where it answered `CONFIRM_ON_MAP`. For NMWC's customers (every location HIGH, 4 to 6 decimals) nothing changes in planning, the demo's locked loads or a re-plan.
  - **Deviations from the design** (each with its reason): (1) the saved point sent back unchanged is checked (confirmed as it is only when verified, or HIGH and inside the company's area; since the A5 review the digits of the stored number are not counted), because the dialog opens on it and saved it as a hand pin, verified HIGH, which would defeat L1 and L4; (2) a "hand pin" exactly on the point of a reading that needs a pin is refused (it was not moved); (3) `GEOCODER` is no longer accepted as a source; (4) `{ input }` alone answers `PIN_REQUIRED`, not `CONFIRM_ON_MAP` (one code; the A2 F17 test changed with it); (5) `PATCH /api/customers/:id` refuses coordinates with 400 instead of dropping them (zod would drop them silently and the page would think it saved); (6) `POST /api/customers`, not named in the design, refuses a pair that needs a pin (422) and one coordinate alone (400; it used to store the one); (7) the import keeps an **existing** customer's saved coordinates when the file's pair needs a pin (the design said leave them empty): a re-import never erases, and an Excel cell that lost its trailing zeros would otherwise turn a good point into LOCATION REQUIRED; since the A5 review it keeps them usable only when the file points at the same place (within the file's precision, or 150 m), else it marks them LOW (kept on the map as the start for the hand pin, blocked like LOCATION REQUIRED); new customers get none, and every such row is listed; (8) a check was added to the legacy run dispatch, which no new plan can reach but old runs can; (9) the day screen, `buildDispatchRequest`, that dispatch and (since the second review) `locationGate` share one predicate, `locationBlocksDelivery`.
  - **Tests** (each fails without its change, checked by reverting it, 19 reverts): web unit `location-rule.spec.ts` (19), `location-rule-routes.spec.ts` (23), `dispatch-location-dialog.spec.ts` +11, `customer-import-locations.spec.ts` +7 (and its F05 tests now use 4-decimal coordinates); integration (library level, real PostgreSQL) `location-rule-db.spec.ts` (7), `master-data-db.spec.ts` (4-decimal coordinates in the F05 race), `dispatch-screen-db.spec.ts` (F17 answers `PIN_REQUIRED`).

With the lock block deleted the deploy fails with P3018 (23502, `depotId` contains null values), checked.

- **A5 third review fixes** (two independent reviewers, 28 Sep 2026; each fix has a test that failed first, and each guard was reverted once to see its test fail):

A PLANNED load could be locked the same way without its RE-PLAN. The proof is the `CUSTOMER_LOCATION_SET` audit row of the change (its "before" point, judged with `locationBlocksDelivery`), so the location route now writes the change and its row in one transaction, and the customer import writes the same row when an exact pair replaces a saved point that was not usable (the import's own remedy says "or fix the file", which led to the same stale stop).
  - **A directions link was read at its start** (medium). `/maps/dir/<start>/<place>/...`: Google puts the start in the path as coordinates when the route starts at "Your location" or a dropped pin, and the path rule took the first waypoint whose coordinates it found, as exact. ADD LOCATION showed it HIGH with Save on, and the server agreed, so the dispatcher's or salesman's own position could be saved as the customer's verified location (three waypoints: the middle one). Now only the end of the route is read, and only when it is a point with a start before it (blank or not); otherwise the link needs a pin (the map centre, MEDIUM, "This directions link does not end at a point..."), or it is not read.
